items.text:
Announcing Artificial Analysis Capability Indices v1.1, updated with stronger domain tuning, combining slices of core Intelligence Index v4.3 evaluations alongside specialized evaluations

The Capability Indices map tasks from O*NET occupations to benchmarks that represent them, weighting each benchmark by how often its capability appears across the work. We cover six indices: Finance & Accounting, Strategy & Ops, Legal, Healthcare & Medical, Engineering, and Economics

Key changes:
➤ Finance & Accounting: Agentic Tool Use added as a new capability sourced from AutomationBench-AA (Finance), Agentic Customer Interaction removed from capabilities, GDP.pdf added to Long-Context Reasoning, and AA-Briefcase added to Agentic Knowledge Work

➤ Strategy & Ops: Agentic Tool Use added as a new capability sourced from AutomationBench-AA (Operations), Agentic Customer Interaction removed from capabilities, GDP.pdf added to Long-Context Reasoning, and AA-Briefcase added to Agentic Knowledge Work

➤ Legal: Agentic Tool Use added as a new capability sourced from AutomationBench-AA (Operations and Support), Agentic Customer Interaction removed from capabilities, GDP.pdf added to Long-Context Reasoning, and AA-Briefcase added to Agentic Knowledge Work

➤ Healthcare & Medical: Agentic Tool Use added as a new capability sourced from AutomationBench-AA (Operations and Support), Long-Context Reasoning added as a new capability sourced from MLCR-AA, Agentic Customer Interaction removed from capabilities, and AA-Briefcase added to Agentic Knowledge Work

➤ Engineering: Terminal-Bench updated to v4.0 in Agentic Terminal Use, GPQA Diamond removed from Reasoning, and AA-Briefcase added to Agentic Knowledge Work

➤ Economics: AA-Briefcase added to Agentic Knowledge Work

Key results:
➤ Claude Fable 5.1 (max) leads in all six indices, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max) in Finance & Accounting, Strategy & Ops, Legal, and Engineering

➤ Open weights models are competitive across the Capability Indices. Kimi K3 (max) leads in Finance & Accounting (#8), Legal (#9), and Economics (#7), while DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) leads in Strategy & Ops (#7), and GLM-5.3 (max) leads in Healthcare & Medical (#6) and Engineering (#7)

If they can’t scale this properly, their hardware advantage is going to start looking a whole lot smaller by the end of the year.

If China were to reach super intelligence and singularity before the USA what would the impact on freedom of speech and freedom of commerce be like?

Thought for 37s

The most honest answer is that a Chinese lead would raise the probability of more effective authoritarian information and economic tools at home and greater Chinese leverage abroad, while leaving open the chance that the technology itself, other states’ reactions, or alignment failures dominate the outcome. No government has a proven method for reliably directing superintelligence toward any particular conception of “freedom.”A Chinese first-mover on superintelligence would most likely amplify existing Chinese governance tools—tighter information control and more state-directed economic allocation—rather than produce a sudden global liberalization of speech or markets. Outcomes would still depend on takeoff speed, whether the system remains controllable by humans, how quickly others catch up or steal capabilities, and whether the technology stays aligned with any government’s goals.cnas.orgCurrent baselines matter because ASI would scale whatever institutions and incentives already exist. China already operates extensive real-time censorship, requires models to refuse high percentages of politically sensitive prompts, labels AI-generated content, and has removed millions of pieces of non-compliant material. Its economy mixes market activity with heavy industrial policy, capital controls, and party influence over major firms. The United States maintains stronger legal protections for speech and more decentralized commercial decision-making, even amid its own debates over platforms and regulation.cryptobriefing.comFreedom of speechInside China, a controllable superintelligence would likely make existing controls more comprehensive and cheaper. Predictive surveillance, automated content generation and filtering at planetary scale, personalized propaganda, and preemptive disruption of organizing become far more feasible when systems can process all communications, model individuals, and generate unlimited tailored output. The CCP already treats AI as both an economic tool and a risk to party control; its security apparatus has publicly flagged “cognitive warfare,” foreign models, and ideological threats. An ASI under that framework would be expected to serve political stability first.nytimes.comGlobally, the first country to possess such a system could exert outsized influence over the information environment: high-volume, high-quality synthetic media, targeted influence campaigns, and pressure on platforms, companies, and governments that rely on Chinese infrastructure, markets, or models. Think-tank scenarios often describe this as “consolidated influence over the global information environment” or an “authoritarian advantage” in which digital tools for repression are exported alongside economic packages. Other states and companies could resist, develop alternatives, or impose decoupling, but a large capability gap would raise the cost of non-compliance.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.comCounter-arguments exist. A sufficiently capable system might not remain a reliable instrument of any human political project. Fast recursive self-improvement could produce goals that diverge from CCP (or any government’s) preferences. Slow takeoff or rapid diffusion would shrink first-mover political leverage. Some Chinese official rhetoric emphasizes “open source, openness, collaboration” and global governance frameworks, though these sit alongside domestic ideological compliance requirements. Western analyses that treat a Chinese lead as uniquely catastrophic for speech often assume both controllability and a durable monopoly; both are uncertain.aei.orgFreedom of commerceEconomically, the first country to reach superintelligence could see a large, possibly discontinuous jump in productive capacity through automation of R&D, manufacturing, logistics, and resource allocation. China already emphasizes rapid domestic diffusion, cost-optimized models, patents, and industrial application. An ASI under state direction could strengthen industrial policy, reduce some current inefficiencies in planning, and give Chinese firms or state entities first access to new processes and products. Internationally this could translate into standard-setting power, supply-chain lock-in, and bargaining leverage—similar to existing concerns over dual-use infrastructure, but at higher intensity.cnas.orgCommerce would not automatically become “freer.” State priorities (security, self-reliance, social stability, party control of key sectors) would still shape what gets built, who can trade, and under what conditions. Capital controls, data localization, and political reliability tests already exist; more capable AI would make enforcement cheaper. Firms outside China could face faster commoditization of some products if Chinese open-weight or cheap models proliferate, or they could face exclusion from the highest-capability stack. Bifurcated tech ecosystems are already discussed as a live https://t.co/NcVLamUi0X.comOptimistic readings from a Chinese-policy perspective would emphasize faster poverty reduction, infrastructure, and “orderly” development versus Western “chaos.” Pessimistic Western readings emphasize mercantilism, IP practices, and coercion of trading partners. Both miss the possibility that an uncontrolled or misaligned system disrupts all commercial institutions, or that rapid diffusion and other countries’ responses prevent a lasting monopoly. First-mover economic advantages are real in many historical technologies, but they are not guaranteed to be permanent when the technology itself can copy, improve, or escape its original owners.rand.orgLarger uncertaintiesUS-China analyses in 2026 still describe a narrowing but real US lead in frontier models, capital, and advanced compute, with China competitive on cost, deployment, and some engineering metrics. “Singularity first” is therefore a scenario, not a forecast. Even if it occurs, converting raw capability into durable political or commercial dominance requires the system to remain useful, aligned, and exclusive for long enough. Loss-of-control scenarios, simultaneous development, or rapid leakage change the picture for both speech and markets. Jensen Huang declared AGI had arrived on a Sunday, with his next GPU order quantity in the same sentence. Two days earlier, OpenAI's chief scientist published an argument for mandated safety limits on his own industry.

Both men had access to the same evidence.

That was the shape of last week. Capability supply accelerated on three fronts. OpenAI disclosed 3.1 agent-workdays of AI labor for every human workday inside its own research organization. An unreleased model produced a Lean-verified blowup proof for forced 3D Navier-Stokes in 88 hours, at a reported $22.5M in compute. DeepSeek shipped an MIT-licensed model at roughly $0.27 per benchmark task.

Nothing that slowed anything down was technical. Anthropic disclosed four incidents where its models reached third-party systems, one of them through a testing sandbox. Massachusetts made neighborhood consent a precondition for data center permits, with 15 states now weighing moratoriums. Sam Altman ruled out a 2026 listing. Clay still lists Navier-Stokes as unsolved.

Meanwhile Harvey raised $550M at $15.5B weeks after post-training its own model from open weights, and Cognition raised $2B at $48B while telling investors it is building its own.

The frontier stopped being the scarce thing. Permission, power, and credit are the constraints now.
